title: Splitting the Weeks We Never Split Evenly
script: Yoga: [tired] Siti, I need to talk about Dad's care schedule. I can't keep taking every single weekend shift.
Siti: [guarded] I did offer to help back in March, if you remember, and you told me you had it handled.
Yoga: [sighing] I know, I know. I underestimated how draining this would become, especially now that his memory is slipping too.
Siti: [carefully] Can I be honest about something that's been sitting with me for weeks?
Yoga: [wary] Go ahead.
Siti: [measured] Growing up, Dad made it fairly obvious you were the one he was proud of, and I was the one he simply tolerated.
Yoga: [defensive] That's not entirely fair, Siti.
Siti: [gently] Maybe not entirely, but it's not entirely untrue either, and I think it's part of why I've hesitated to volunteer more.
Yoga: [quiet] I never realized you carried that around all this time.
Siti: [reflective] I didn't want it to sound like an accusation. I'm telling you because I still want to help, in spite of it.
Yoga: [surprised] In spite of it? I would have understood if you'd stayed away entirely.
Siti: [thoughtful] I considered that, honestly. But whatever he did or didn't give me as a father, caring for him now isn't a debt he gets to collect or cancel.
Yoga: [moved] That's a more generous way of looking at it than I would have managed, in your position.
Siti: [sincere] It's not generosity toward him, really. It's more that I don't want to become someone who only shows up where love was shown to her first.
Yoga: [thoughtful] So where does that leave us, practically speaking?
Siti: [determined] Split the week evenly, starting this Saturday. I'll take Tuesdays and Thursdays, you keep the weekends, and we split appointments as they come up.
Yoga: [relieved] That sounds fair. More than fair, actually, given everything you've just told me.
Siti: [warmly] It's fair to him too, which matters more to me than it being fair between us.
Yoga: [quietly] Thank you, Siti. I don't think I ever properly said that.
Siti: [gently] You don't need to. Just show up on Tuesday and let me sleep in for once.

quiz.question: Why does Yoga say he can't keep taking every weekend shift?
options: He is moving to another city
He is exhausted and their father's memory is slipping too
He no longer wants to help
He has a new job
quiz.explanation: Yoga admits he underestimated how draining it would become, especially with their father's memory now slipping.

quiz.question: What does Siti reveal about their childhood?
options: Their father treated them exactly the same
Their father was clearly prouder of Yoga while merely tolerating her
She was the favorite child
Their father ignored both of them
quiz.explanation: Siti says their father made it obvious Yoga was the one he was proud of, while she was simply tolerated.

quiz.question: Why does Siti say she still wants to help despite that history?
options: She wants their father's inheritance
Caring for him now isn't a debt he gets to collect or cancel
Yoga forced her to help
She feels guilty about the past
quiz.explanation: She explains that whatever their father did or didn't give her, caring for him now isn't a debt he can collect or cancel.

quiz.question: What arrangement do Siti and Yoga agree on?
options: Yoga will handle everything alone
Siti takes Tuesdays and Thursdays, Yoga keeps weekends, and they split appointments
They will hire a stranger
Siti will take over completely
quiz.explanation: They agree to split the week evenly: Siti takes Tuesdays and Thursdays, Yoga keeps weekends, and appointments are split.

quiz.question: Why does Siti say the fairness matters more to their father than between the siblings?
options: She wants credit for being generous
Because that priority matters more to her than fairness between herself and Yoga
She wants Yoga to feel guilty
She doesn't actually think it's fair
quiz.explanation: Siti says the arrangement being fair to their father matters more to her than it being fair between the two of them.
